projectDetails.name: Project Orbit Sentinel
projectDetails.details:
1) Introduction

Protecting the explorers. Empowering the future.

Space exploration is not only about how far humanity can go, but how well we can protect those who take us there. As astronauts venture into deep space, they face challenges that extend far beyond Earth: radiation exposure, altered gravity, physical deterioration, sleep disruption, and psychological stress. With limited access to immediate medical support, monitoring their own health becomes essential. Orbit Sentinel is an astronaut health monitoring platform designed to bring these critical indicators together in one intelligent interface. By tracking vital signs, radiation exposure, sleep, mental well-being, and physical performance, while connecting gravitational conditions to the body's adaptation, it helps astronauts understand their health, recognize potential risks, and make informed decisions throughout their missions.

Because the future of space exploration depends not only on reaching new worlds, but on keeping humanity healthy enough to explore them.

2) Radiation

Space radiation is one of the most significant health challenges in human space exploration, particularly during long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. Orbit Sentinel doesn't just monitor radiation. It helps astronauts understand exposure, respond to alerts, and follow protective procedures, even when Earth is far away. Is designed to transform scientific radiation measurements into actionable health-monitoring information, combining NASA radiation datasets, automated data processing, exposure visualization, and mission-specific safety guidance.

2.1. Integration with NASA Radiation Data - Real Scientific Measurements

Orbit Sentinel's proposed radiation monitoring architecture integrates with NASA's Radiation Laboratory (RadLab) API, part of NASA's Open Science Data Repository ecosystem. This integration enables the application to retrieve historical radiation measurements collected by scientific instruments aboard spacecraft, including the International Space Station (ISS). Using NASA's documented API, the system can query radiation data according to spacecraft, instrument, measurement type, and observation period.

2.2 Example NASA API endpoint:

https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/api/?spacecraft=ISS&instrument=DosTel&timestamp%3E=2022-04-01T23%3A00&timestamp%3C2022-04-02T01%3A05&dose_equivalent_rate&format=json

This request is designed to retrieve dose-equivalent-rate measurements from the DosTel instrument for a specified historical period. By incorporating NASA's scientific datasets, Orbit Sentinel aims to demonstrate how actual space radiation observations can support astronaut health-monitoring applications, reducing dependence on exclusively simulated measurements.

2.3 Radiation Data Processing - Backend Architecture

Orbit Sentinel uses a proposed backend architecture to process, standardize, and organize radiation measurements. The backend acts as an intermediary between external scientific data sources and the astronaut-facing monitoring interface. Its processing workflow consists of five stages:

  1. Data Acquisition: Retrieve radiation measurements from NASA RadLab or other compatible sources.
  2. Data Validation: Verify measurement availability, timestamps, units, instrument identification, and data integrity.
  3. Unit Standardization: Convert compatible radiation measurements into standardized units for consistent presentation.
  4. Exposure Monitoring: Organize measurements into historical time series and calculate exposure trends.
  5. API Distribution: Deliver structured JSON responses to the Orbit Sentinel dashboard.

This modular architecture is intended to support additional radiation monitoring instruments in the future, including compatible personal dosimeters and spacecraft radiation sensors, subject to their communication protocols and data-access permissions.

2.4 Radiation Calculations - Transforming Scientific Data into Structured JSON

One of Orbit Sentinel's key technical capabilities is its proposed radiation data-processing pipeline. NASA RadLab can provide dose-equivalent-rate measurements expressed in microsieverts per hour (µSv/h). When this measurement is available, the Laravel backend converts it into millisieverts per hour (mSv/h) using the following equation: Dose Rate (mSv/h) = Dose Rate (µSv/h) / 1,000

For example, a hypothetical measurement of 14 µSv/h produces: 14 / 1,000 = 0.014 mSv/h

This standardized measurement can then be displayed in the astronaut's radiation monitoring dashboard. For time-series measurements, accumulated dose can be estimated by integrating the dose-equivalent rate over time: Accumulated Dose (mSv) ≈ Σ [Dose Rate (mSv/h) × Time Interval (hours)]

This calculation requires valid measurement intervals and consistent dosimetric quantities. It does not automatically represent an astronaut's total mission exposure unless the relevant personal exposure history is available. After processing, the backend is designed to expose a standardized REST endpoint:

GET /api/radiation/latest

Example JSON response: {  "source": "nasa_radlab",  "spacecraft": "ISS",  "instrument": DosTel",  "measurement": { "quantity": "dose_equivalent_rate", "value": 0.014, "unit": "mSv/h"  },  "mission_dose_mSv": null,  "status": "not_evaluated",  "sensor_status": "unknown",  "alert": null,  "data_mode": "historical",  "is_simulated": false}

This JSON illustrates the proposed data transformation using a hypothetical measurement, not a verified API response.

The structured response allows the frontend to consume radiation information independently of the original scientific data format. It also distinguishes historical measurements from simulated data and avoids assigning safety classifications when validated mission-specific thresholds are unavailable.

2.5 Radiation Monitoring and Astronaut Decision Support

Orbit Sentinel is designed to go beyond radiation data visualization by connecting exposure measurements with astronaut health-monitoring workflows. Its radiation monitoring interface is structured around four complementary capabilities:

2.6 Continuous Exposure Visualization

Display the latest available radiation measurements, historical trends, and accumulated exposure when sufficient data exists.

2.7 Radiation Alerts

Evaluate incoming measurements against configurable, mission-approved exposure criteria and identify potentially abnormal changes. In the demonstration environment, simulated radiation events can trigger illustrative alerts without representing operational NASA safety thresholds.

2.8 Health Symptom Reporting

Connect radiation monitoring with the Orbit Sentinel Report Symptoms module, enabling astronauts to document symptoms, record their onset and severity, and associate reports with available exposure measurements for subsequent medical review.

The application does not assume that symptoms are caused by radiation exposure and does not replace medical diagnosis or mission medical protocols.

2.9 Protective Action Guidance

Provide astronauts with offline-accessible guidance based on mission-approved radiation protection procedures, including shelter instructions and communication protocols during potential radiation events.

2.10 Technical Innovation and Mission Impact

The central innovation of Orbit Sentinel is not the radiation sensor itself, but the software architecture that transforms complex scientific measurements into accessible information for astronaut health monitoring. Orbit Sentinel's vision is to turn space radiation data into meaningful, timely, and actionable information, helping astronauts monitor their exposure, recognize potential hazards, and follow appropriate protective procedures during missions beyond Earth.

3) Isolation and Confinement

During long-duration space missions, astronauts face significant behavioral and psychological challenges caused by prolonged isolation, confinement in limited spaces, and separation from Earth. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel integrates digital tools designed to monitor mental well-being, sleep patterns, emotional states, and fatigue. Through daily check-ins, visual health indicators, and personalized recommendations, the platform helps astronauts recognize behavioral changes, maintain healthy routines, and take preventive action. Our goal is to transform health monitoring into proactive support, strengthening astronaut resilience, well-being, and autonomy throughout deep-space missions.

3.1 Sleep Monitoring - Last Night

Orbit Sentinel provides a detailed overview of the astronaut's latest sleep cycle, including total sleep duration, sleep quality, and estimated sleep stages (Deep, Light, REM, and Awake). The system highlights irregular sleep routines and offers practical recommendations to encourage consistent rest patterns, helping astronauts recognize potential sleep-related risks during prolonged missions.

3.2 Sleep Trends - 7-Day Analysis

The seven-day dashboard tracks sleep duration over time, displaying average sleep hours, daily variations, and progress toward rest goals. Visual trends help astronauts identify changes in their sleeping habits, while contextual recommendations encourage healthier routines and greater awareness of potential fatigue.

3.3 Daily Check-in - Emotional Self-Assessment

A simple, intuitive interface allows astronauts to record how they feel through five emotional states: Great, Good, Normal, Tired, and Bad. Additional fields capture energy levels and physical symptoms, creating a daily record of self-reported health that can help astronauts recognize changes in their emotional and physical condition.

3.4 Mental Health - Psychological Well-being

Orbit Sentinel brings together four essential psychological indicators: Mood, Stress, Fatigue, and Focus, presented through an intuitive well-being dashboard. A visual well-being score provides a quick overview of the astronaut's reported mental state, supporting self-awareness and encouraging regular emotional check-ins. By tracking these indicators over time, the system aims to help astronauts recognize early signs of psychological strain associated with isolation and confinement.

Our Goal: Transform daily health observations into meaningful insights, helping astronauts maintain emotional resilience, healthy sleep routines, and psychological well-being throughout long-duration space missions.

4) Distance from Earth

As astronauts travel farther from Earth, communication delays increase, reducing the ability of mission control teams to provide immediate assistance during medical emergencies. This challenge becomes particularly significant during long-duration missions to Mars, where one-way communication delays can reach approximately 20 minutes. Orbit Sentinel addresses this NASA Human Research Program hazard by providing a simulated Distance from Earth monitoring module that demonstrates how increasing distance affects communication availability and astronaut autonomy.

The goal is to transform mission-distance scenarios into meaningful operational information, helping astronauts understand communication limitations and the importance of autonomous decision-making during deep-space missions.

4.1 NASA Hazard Alignment - Distance from Earth

According to NASA's Human Research Program, distance from Earth introduces significant challenges to human space exploration, including delayed communication, limited access to immediate medical support, equipment failures, and the need for greater crew self-sufficiency.

The module focuses on two primary indicators:

a) Earth Distance: Represents the simulated distance between the spacecraft and Earth, displayed in miles.

b) One-Way Signal Delay: Represents the estimated time required for a radio signal to travel from the spacecraft to Earth, based on the simulated distance and the speed of light.

Orbit Sentinel uses this hazard as the foundation for its Distance from Earth module.

Orbit Sentinel provides an interactive mission dashboard that visualizes the spacecraft's journey between Earth and Mars, displaying distance traveled, remaining distance, estimated arrival time, and one-way communication delay.

5) Gravity Fields

During space missions, astronauts must adapt to different gravitational environments, from microgravity during spaceflight to the partial gravity of Mars. These changes can affect muscle strength, bone density, balance, coordination, and cardiovascular function. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel provides integrated tools designed to monitor physical condition, track exercise routines, and support adaptation to changing gravity. Through visual health indicators, activity tracking, and preventive recommendations, the platform helps astronauts maintain physical readiness and recognize potential changes in their condition.

Our goal is to support physical resilience, reduce the risks associated with altered gravity, and help astronauts remain healthy and mission-ready throughout their journey.

5.1 Physical Condition - Health and Performance Monitoring

Orbit Sentinel provides a unified overview of the astronaut's physical condition, including exercise load, muscle and bone status, balance, and cardiovascular capacity. A seven-day activity chart helps visualize physical performance trends, while clear status indicators allow astronauts to quickly assess their condition and maintain awareness of their physical readiness.

5.2 Bone & Balance - Musculoskeletal Health

In reduced gravity, maintaining muscle strength and bone health becomes essential. Orbit Sentinel tracks resistance exercise sessions, displays completed and planned activities, and provides indicators for bone loading and muscle condition. By organizing exercise routines and monitoring activity consistency, the platform supports astronauts in maintaining musculoskeletal health and following their physical conditioning plans.

5.3 Gravity Fields - Adaptation to Martian Gravity

Transitioning between gravitational environments presents unique challenges for astronaut health and mobility. Orbit Sentinel includes a dedicated gravity adaptation dashboard that displays the current mission environment, including Mars' gravitational acceleration of approximately 0.38 g.bThe interface highlights four key adaptation areas: Balance, Coordination, Muscle Strength, and Bone Health, providing a consolidated overview of physical readiness.

Preventive recommendations encourage regular exercise and awareness of symptoms such as dizziness or balance difficulties, supporting safer adaptation to partial-gravity environments.

6) Hostile/Closed Environments

During long-duration space missions, maintaining a safe and healthy environment inside a spacecraft is essential. Astronauts face challenges related to air quality, atmospheric pressure, temperature, microbial contamination, lighting, and noise, all of which can affect their health and performance. To address these challenges, Orbit Sentinel introduces a dedicated habitat monitoring dashboard designed to provide astronauts with a clear overview of their living environment.

6.1 Habitat Environment - Environmental Health Monitoring

Orbit Sentinel brings together essential environmental indicators in a single, intuitive interface:

  • Air Quality: Displays oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels to support awareness of atmospheric conditions.
  • Cabin Conditions: Presents temperature and atmospheric pressure readings to help astronauts assess their living environment.
  • Microbial Monitoring: Provides visibility into the monitoring status of microbial conditions in cabin air and surfaces.
  • Lighting & Noise: Displays environmental status indicators related to crew comfort and well-being.

Through clear visual indicators and environmental status summaries, the platform helps astronauts quickly recognize potential changes in habitat conditions.

Our goal is to transform complex environmental information into accessible insights, supporting astronaut safety, environmental awareness, and informed decision-making during deep-space missions.

challengeDetails.title: The Earth Information Jukebox
challengeDetails.excerpt: NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) produces stunning visualizations of our changing planet, but presenting Earth science through visualization alone limits who can reach it. projectDetails.name: Mission Mars Game
projectDetails.summary: Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer that lets a child run a Mars colony for eleven sols. Five resources — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — rise and fall in real time while the colony moves through 90-second days and nights. Twenty-five events, from dust storms and marsquakes to crew conflicts, appear in a Mission Log with four trade-off choices each, and ignoring one has its own consequence. Buildings have levels and build timers, research takes time, robots explore the surface and can break down, and a radio link to Houston answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way real deep-space communication does. Every event, site and term is tagged with the open NASA source behind it: DONKI space weather, OSDR life sciences, Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight and SCaN. Losing opens a science debriefing instead of a "game over", so failure becomes a lesson. Three difficulty modes let younger and older players train at their own pace. Mars is the hook; systems thinking is the lesson.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works. Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer where a child commands a Mars colony for eleven sols. The screen is a mission control center: a header with the mission clock and a day/night indicator, a COLONY RESOURCES panel with five live bars — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — and a Mission Log that is the heart of the game. Every event appears there as a large Mars image, a timestamp, a short narrative and four big decision buttons. Time runs on a fixed cycle: 90 seconds of daylight and 90 seconds of night, three minutes per sol. Solar panels produce energy only in daylight, batteries carry the base through the night, and the crew keeps consuming water, oxygen and food the whole time. Twenty-five events are drawn at random and weighted toward pressure — 20% opportunities, 40% dilemmas, 40% crises — and every one of them has four choices with real trade-offs, hidden risks and a consequence if the player ignores the event for 60 seconds. Buildings have five levels and take time to build or upgrade. Ten research technologies reach three levels each and cost 30, 60 or 90 seconds per level. Robots with 100 hit points are built, sent to twenty real Martian sites such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia and Olympus Mons, and can break down and be repaired or lost. A radio link to Houston costs energy and answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way deep-space communication really works. Winning means surviving to sol 11 and returning to Earth; losing opens a science debriefing that explains the cause, what was learned and one tip for the next flight.

Benefits and intended impact. The game teaches systems thinking: saving energy can starve oxygen, a fast trip can cost a robot, and a party raises morale but eats the food stores. Children practice reading trends, comparing costs and asking for help before an emergency grows — with no penalty for failing, because every loss is explained. It also makes open NASA data a story kids can touch, and it runs in any browser on a school computer or tablet with nothing to install.

Tools and languages. React 19 with TypeScript and TanStack Start, styled with Tailwind CSS v4. The whole simulation is one pure reducer in a single engine file, so every tab reads the same state and every rule can be unit-tested; 106 automated tests cover resource flow, death rules, research, robots, exploration, radio support and difficulty. Event art is generated imagery, and the project was built and iterated with Lovable.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz or a score, failure is rewritten as a debriefing; instead of instant answers, the radio reproduces real signal latency; instead of a "correct" option, each choice is only better or worse for the colony you actually have.

Factors considered. Difficulty for ages 7–12 without unfair punishment, honest sourcing of NASA data, screen simplicity and large touch targets, three difficulty modes, and no names, faces or voices of anyone under 18 anywhere in the project.

The file also has a ≈250-word version, the NASA data links for those fields, and a pre-paste checklist. I ran the tests to confirm the numbers quoted: 106 passing, 25 events, 20 sites, 10 researches, 8 buildings, 15–20 s radio delay.

projectDetails.details:
Earth System Detective, developed by Team Startec – SESI Araguari, is an interactive web application designed to make Earth observation data more accessible and understandable.

The platform allows users to investigate environmental changes by selecting variables, geographic locations and time periods. It presents information through interactive maps, time-series charts and statistical indicators, including the Mann–Kendall test, Sen's slope and linear regression. Users can also download reports in CSV, TXT and PDF formats for further analysis.

The current application uses real, open NASA POWER data, including relative humidity and evapotranspiration variables. These resources help users explore environmental patterns and investigate whether changes over time show statistically significant trends.

The project was developed as a web application using Lovable and Lovable Cloud, with AI-assisted tools supporting code generation, interface development, debugging and testing. ChatGPT also supported scientific research, statistical methodology, documentation and project planning.

Our creative approach is to transform complex scientific datasets into an interactive investigation experience. Instead of simply displaying environmental information, the application encourages users to ask questions, select locations, explore evidence and interpret results.

The intended impact is to support environmental education, scientific literacy and informed discussions about changes in Earth's systems, particularly among students, educators and communities.

Throughout development, we considered scientific validity, data quality, traceability, spatial and temporal resolution, accessibility, transparency and responsible interpretation of statistical results. We also ensured that simulated information would not be presented as real NASA observations.

The MODIS NDVI module is part of our planned expansion. Its interface and processing workflow have been developed, but official MODIS files have not yet been imported and validated. Therefore, NDVI results are not currently presented as verified scientific findings.

projectDetails.name: "TREM" DE FERRO: Minas Gerais Banded Iron Formations as Geochemical Analogs for Martian ISRU
projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive web platform and in situ resource utilization (ISRU) simulator benchmarking the Banded Iron Formations (BIFs) of Brazil's Iron Quadrangle (Minas Gerais) as functional geochemical analogs for hematite-rich Martian regolith at Meridiani Planum and Gale Crater. Our solution moves beyond surface visual resemblances with terrestrial deserts by targeting mineral extraction. Based on the fundamental reduction reaction (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂), we model two mature metallurgical pathways—Hydrogen Direct Reduction (DRI-H₂) and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE)—to co-produce breathable life-support oxygen, rocket propellant, and structural metallic iron for additive habitat manufacturing. This work addresses a primary constraint of deep space missions: return propellant (LOX) represents the single largest mass penalty from Earth (~25 metric tons for a four-person crew under NASA DRA 5.0). Testing these processing routes using Minas Gerais ores enables early calibration of specific energy consumption, chemical yields, and equipment reliability in terrestrial pilot facilities before launching payloads to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
"TREM" DE FERRO is an open-access web platform and ISRU simulator establishing a functional and geochemical bridge between terrestrial Banded Iron Formations (itabirites and hematites from Minas Gerais, Brazil) and Martian iron-oxide deposits identified by NASA rovers. Rather than seeking morphological desert analogs, we target chemical and mineral parity: extracting oxygen and metallic iron from ferric oxide (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂). The platform models two core industrial pathways: Hydrogen Direct Reduction (DRI-H₂), which thermochemically reduces ore into sponge iron and water vapor before recovering H₂ through water electrolysis, and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE), which electrochemically cracks molten iron oxide at ~1,600 °C directly into pure liquid iron and gaseous oxygen without requiring water.

The primary benefit is substantially derisking surface operations and reducing launch mass. According to NASA’s Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0 (DRA 5.0), return descent/ascent vehicles require approximately 25 metric tons of liquid oxygen (LOX). While NASA’s MOXIE experiment proved that atmospheric oxygen generation works, it produced 122 grams total throughout its mission. Sustained surface habitats require regolith mineral processing. By benchmarking processing routes in Minas Gerais pilot facilities, researchers can validate specific energy consumption (kWh/kg O₂), powder fluidization, and reduction kinetics on Earth prior to flight hardware fabrication.

The interactive platform was developed using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and custom numerical models for stoichiometric and thermodynamic balances. Planetary datasets were retrieved from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) Geosciences and Atmospheres nodes, integrating APXS/CheMin spectrometry from Curiosity, PIXL data from Perseverance, Mössbauer hematite spectra from Opportunity, and MOXIE operational telemetry. Terrestrial geological grades and mineralogical baselines were sourced from CPRM/Geological Survey of Brazil (SGB) database surveys.

Our key conceptual shift was discarding passive landscape analogies in favor of active geochemical and metallurgical testing. Brazil possesses one of the world's most advanced mining and direct-reduction industrial ecosystems; mobilizing this infrastructure as an accessible proving ground for space exploration turns a major terrestrial industry into an operational asset for Mars.

The team established an explicit boundary for the analogy: what can be directly validated on Earth (dry magnetic pre-concentration efficiency, reduction kinetics, and thermodynamic efficiency) versus what strictly requires environmental simulation chambers (0.38 g Martian gravity, a 6 hPa CO₂ atmosphere, and reactive perchlorate salts in the regolith).

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: CrewVitals
projectDetails.summary: CrewVitals is a web app that lets an astronaut on a long mission check their own health in about a minute a day. The crew member logs six indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood. The app compares each reading with a clinical reference range, shows a green, yellow or red status with plain-language guidance, tracks trends across mission days, and says when a result should go to the Crew Medical Officer or the flight surgeon on the ground. A clickable body map explains how spaceflight affects each body system, with every statement linked to its NASA source. A radiation panel compares dose rates measured by real instruments in six environments, from the International Space Station to the surface of Mars, and a banner reports recent solar events, all from NASA databases. On missions far from Earth, communication with the ground is delayed and crews carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in their own health. CrewVitals is built for that situation.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

  • Daily check-in. One short form for six indicators, with a note beside each field on how to take the measurement. A status badge updates as the crew member types.
  • Dashboard. The mission day, an overall status, and one card per indicator with the reading, its position against the reference range, and what to do next.
  • Guidance and escalation. Green means keep the routine. Yellow gives self-care steps and asks for a new reading the next day. Red gives the next step for that indicator and says when to inform the Crew Medical Officer. A red trend goes to the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon on the ground. A small set of critical values triggers an urgent message.
  • Trends. One chart per indicator across mission days, with the reference band shaded and out-of-range days marked. Four trend rules look at three consecutive days, for example sleep under six hours three nights in a row, and raise an alert that a single reading would not.
  • Body map. A figure with six regions. Selecting a region shows its latest readings, how spaceflight affects that body system, the related hazards of human spaceflight, related open-science studies, and the reason for tracking it.
  • Radiation across six environments. The radiation panel shows absorbed dose measured on the same day, 1 December 2022, by instruments on the ISS, in lunar orbit, inside the Orion capsule during Artemis I, in deep space, in Mars orbit and on the surface of Mars. The crew member can select each one to see its dose rate through the day. The panel states that the instruments differ in design, shielding and location, so the values are what each instrument measured and not comparable crew doses.
  • Space weather. A banner reports solar flares and solar energetic particle events from the last seven days.
  • Mission setting. The crew member chooses ISS, Lunar surface or Mars transit. On Mars transit, every instruction that sends the crew to the ground adds a reminder that communication is delayed and the onboard procedure comes first. The panel also says plainly where no measured data exists for the chosen setting.
  • Two languages. The app opens in English and can be switched to Brazilian Portuguese with one selector. Links to NASA pages are marked as English-language pages when the app is in Portuguese.
  • Demo mission. One button loads 30 days of simulated crew data, clearly labelled as simulated, so the trends and alerts can be seen at once.

How it works

CrewVitals is a single-page web app that runs in the browser. Health entries are stored only on the device, in the browser's local storage, and nothing the crew member types is sent to a server. Status rules and reference ranges live in one file, so a flight surgeon could review or replace them in one place. Three small server functions fetch NASA data and fall back to a saved copy when a source is unavailable. The app always shows whether NASA data is live or a saved snapshot, and always labels simulated crew data.

What we were careful about

  • The alert thresholds are adult clinical reference ranges used on Earth, and the app says so on every card. We did not invent spaceflight-specific thresholds. They were reviewed by the team's biomedical engineer.
  • NASA statements are paraphrased and shown with a link to the NASA page they come from. A team member checked each paraphrase against its NASA source. The team's own reasoning is shown separately and labelled as ours.
  • No environment is presented as another. There is no measured lunar-surface or Mars-transit radiation data in the source database, and the app says so instead of substituting a different environment.
  • Status is never shown by colour alone. Each status has an icon and a text label. An automated accessibility check reports no violations on any screen.
  • The app is a hackathon prototype and not a medical device, and it says so on every page.

Benefits and goals

On a Mars mission a message to the ground can take up to 20 minutes to arrive, and the answer as long to come back. A crew member needs a tool that helps them notice a change early, tells them what they can do themselves, and makes clear when to involve the crew's medical officer. Our goal was a tool simple enough to use every day and honest about what it knows. Next steps would be readings taken directly from onboard medical devices, thresholds set by flight surgeons, and a personal radiation dose record fed by the crew member's own dosimeter.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, React Router, Lucide icons, Vitest. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages with Pages Functions. Source code: https://github.com/pedronogueira21/crewvitals

How we used NASA and partner data

  • NASA Human Research Program, "5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight": the frame for the whole app. Each indicator and body region is linked to the hazards that affect it.
  • NASA, "The Human Body in Space": source of the paraphrased statements in the body map.
  • NASA RadLab (Open Science Data Repository): absorbed dose rates for one common day, 1 December 2022, from six instruments: ISS (DosTel1), lunar orbit (LRO, CRaTER), inside Orion on Artemis I (HERA), deep space (BioSentinel, BPD), Mars orbit (TGO, Liulin-MO) and Mars surface (Curiosity, MSL-RAD).
  • NASA CCMC DONKI: recent solar flares and solar energetic particle events for the space-weather banner.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository search: related open-science studies for each indicator, shown with organism and study type because many are animal or ground studies.
  • ESA: the Mars-orbit measurements come from the Liulin-MO dosimeter on the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint ESA–Roscosmos mission. We accessed them through NASA's RadLab database.
  • The alert ranges are adapted from ACC/AHA blood pressure categories and American Diabetes Association glucose criteria.

Use of AI

The application code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by the team. Claude also helped plan the project and drafted the interface text, the paraphrases of NASA pages (each checked by a team member against its source), the Portuguese translation and the demo slides. Gemini (Google) was used as an aid in the clinical review, which the team's biomedical engineer approved. The body map figure and the app icon are simple schematics drawn in code with AI assistance, identified as such in the app. The demo mission is simulated data and is labelled as simulated. No NASA logos or mission identifiers are used.

projectDetails.name: Project Ares
projectDetails.summary:
Project Ares is a pixel-art game, in Portuguese and English, where children aged 7 to 12 command a mission to Mars: a 180-day journey and 10 sols at the base. Each turn, players split limited energy (8 points, only 4 during a dust storm) among air and water, greenhouse, radiation shield and radio, which sends science to Earth (goal: 30). Decision cards offer two options, and both have a cost; the active option leads to a 15-second minigame. Crew members Lia, Davi and Yara have their own bonuses, and the robot Orbi guides the tutorial. The ending is punishment-free: a 1-to-3-star debriefing and a certificate with the player’s name.

The game answers the challenge of teaching real space engineering decisions to young learners: energy is limited and every system competes for the same resources. It uses real NASA data: radiation measured by the Curiosity rover and 1,036 solar flares from 2024 in the DONKI archive. The storm warning only arrives with the radio on, forcing a choice between science and safety. The data is archived and shown with its date and source. The game rules are separate from the interface and covered by automated tests.

It matters because children learn through consequences: they discover why radiation is the biggest obstacle on the way to Mars and how engineers decide under uncertainty. It is free, bilingual, accessible (keyboard, screen reader, optional minigames) and runs in any browser, reaching schools and families at no cost.
projectDetails.details:
Project Ares is an interactive, bilingual educational browser game that simulates the challenges of a human mission to Mars. Designed for children aged 7 to 12, it combines pixel-art visuals, storytelling, resource management, and interactive minigames to make space science more engaging and accessible.

How It Works

Players take command of a three-member astronaut crew: Lia, the commander; Davi, the engineer; and Yara, the botanist. Each character has a unique bonus, while Orbi, a companion robot, guides players through the tutorial and provides contextual hints throughout the experience.

The gameplay is divided into two phases: a 180-day journey to Mars, represented by six turns, followed by ten Martian sols at the base. During each turn, players manage a limited energy supply generated by solar panels, allocating resources among four essential systems: air and water, greenhouse food production, radiation protection, and radio communications. Players must balance crew survival with scientific research, aiming to transmit 30 science points back to Earth.

Random events introduce additional challenges through decision cards with two possible outcomes. Each active decision leads to a short minigame that can improve or worsen its result. The experience concludes with a non-punitive performance assessment, encouraging players to learn from their decisions and try again.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Project Ares promotes scientific literacy, critical thinking, strategic planning, and resource management. Rather than presenting space science through passive explanations, it allows children to understand scientific concepts through consequences and experimentation.

The game incorporates authentic NASA information, including radiation measurements collected by the Curiosity rover, solar flare records from NASA's DONKI database, and references to real technologies and missions such as the ISS water recycling system, Perseverance's MOXIE experiment, and the Opportunity rover.

This approach helps children understand the real difficulties of space exploration, particularly radiation exposure, environmental hazards, energy limitations, and the importance of scientific communication. The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about science, technology, engineering, and space exploration from an early age.

Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: Page structure and game interface.
  • CSS3: Visual design, pixel-art presentation, animations, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript: Gameplay mechanics, resource management, event systems, character bonuses, and minigames.
  • Python: Data collection and processing scripts for NASA datasets.
  • Node.js Test Runner: Approximately 25 automated tests covering the core game logic.
  • Vercel: Deployment and hosting, providing public access to the game.
  • NASA Open Data: Scientific datasets and mission information used to support gameplay accuracy.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control, source code management, and collaborative development.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/germanoafb/Base_Mars

The architecture separates the game rules from the user interface, making the system easier to maintain, test, and expand. The game runs directly in the browser without requiring installation.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Project Ares lies in transforming complex scientific information into meaningful gameplay mechanics. Radiation exposure, solar storms, energy scarcity, and scientific communication are not merely background details; they directly influence player decisions and mission outcomes.

For example, maintaining radio communications allows players to receive early warnings about solar storms, creating a strategic trade-off between scientific progress and crew safety. Similarly, radiation protection requires careful resource allocation, demonstrating why shielding is essential for long-duration space missions.

The combination of pixel-art aesthetics, character-driven storytelling, interactive minigames, and real scientific data creates an educational experience that connects entertainment with authentic scientific challenges.

Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: NASA data is presented with its original dates and sources, without being misrepresented as real-time information.
  • Age-appropriate design: Mechanics, language, and visual elements are designed for children aged 7–12.
  • Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatibility, reduced-motion support, and the ability to skip minigames.
  • Educational value: Every major gameplay mechanic reinforces a scientific concept or encourages strategic thinking.
  • Fairness and engagement: The non-punitive ending encourages experimentation and learning rather than discouraging players for making mistakes.
  • Accessibility of technology: Free hosting, browser compatibility, and bilingual support make the experience available to schools and families without additional costs.

Ultimately, Project Ares aims to demonstrate that scientific education can be interactive, inclusive, and entertaining while remaining grounded in real-world research. It invites children to experience the challenges of Mars exploration and inspires them to think like scientists, engineers, and explorers.
